helios.transcript:
Interviewer (Dana): Thanks for the time, Marcus. Can you describe what Verdant Grid set out to build this year?

Subject (Marcus Lindqvist, CTO): Sure. We build controllers for residential solar microgrids — neighbourhoods where a lot of homes have rooftop solar and a battery, all tied together. This year's project was a predictive load-balancing controller. The goal was to keep voltage stable across the cluster while shifting load and battery charge/discharge around, so no single feeder gets overloaded when everyone's exporting at noon or pulling hard at dinner.

Dana: What made that hard? Couldn't you just use standard grid controls?

Marcus: The standard stuff assumes a central operator and predictable one-way power flow. Our situation is the opposite — power flows both directions, generation is intermittent, and there's no central meter we can trust in real time. The big unknown was whether we could forecast cluster-level net load accurately enough to act ahead of a voltage event, given how fast cloud cover changes generation. We genuinely didn't know if a useful forecast was even possible at the timescale we needed.

Dana: So what did you try?

Marcus: First we tried a rule-based controller — thresholds on voltage that triggered battery dispatch. It oscillated badly; batteries fought each other across homes and we got voltage flicker. So that approach told us coordination had to be predictive, not reactive. Then we built a forecasting model off historical generation and weather, and drove dispatch from the forecast. That was better in steady conditions but fell apart during fast partial-cloud transitions — the forecast lagged reality. The third iteration was a distributed approach where each home's controller negotiates with its neighbours instead of relying on a central forecast. That held voltage much better, but it introduced a new problem: the negotiation could fail to converge when comms latency spiked.

Dana: Where did it land?

Marcus: We've got the distributed negotiation working in simulation and on a small bench setup. Voltage stays within band in most scenarios. The open question we're still chasing is convergence guarantees under degraded communications — we don't yet know the conditions where it's provably stable. And honestly there's a lot of homeowner-app polish we did too, the dashboard and notifications, which took a chunk of time. But the core controller is the real work.

Dana: Anything on results?

Marcus: In sim, the distributed controller cut voltage excursions by about two-thirds versus the rule-based baseline. That's the headline. The convergence-under-latency thing is next year's problem.

cedarline.transcript:
Interviewer (Jordan Ellis): Thanks for making the time, Priya. For the record, can you describe what Cedarline Systems set out to build this fiscal year?

Subject (Priya Shah, Controls Lead): Sure. We make control units for mid-size cold storage warehouses, the kind that hold produce and pharmaceuticals between two and eight degrees. This year we tried to build a controller that keeps every zone inside a half-degree band while the load changes through the day. Doors open, pallets of warm product come in, compressors cycle, and the building never behaves the same way twice.

Interviewer (Jordan Ellis): What did the market already offer, and why was that not enough?

Subject (Priya Shah, Controls Lead): The standard approach is a PID loop per zone with fixed tuning. It works when the load is steady. Our customers told us that during receiving hours the product temperature drifted by two to three degrees, which is enough to fail a pharmaceutical audit. We looked at the published tuning methods and the vendor application notes. None of them told us how to handle zones that interact. When zone three pulls hard, zone four loses capacity because they share a compressor rack.

Interviewer (Jordan Ellis): So what was the technical question you could not answer at the start?

Subject (Priya Shah, Controls Lead): We did not know whether we could separate the effect of each operating variable on the temperature response. Door openings, product mass, compressor staging and defrost cycles all change at once. Standard tuning assumes one input and one output. We did not know if a model of the coupling could be identified from normal operating data, or if we would need to disturb the system on purpose to learn it.

Interviewer (Jordan Ellis): How did you go about it?

Subject (Priya Shah, Controls Lead): First we established a baseline with the existing controller at our test site in Abbotsford, a twelve-zone warehouse. We logged every sensor at one-second resolution for three weeks. Then we held the configuration constant and changed one operating condition at a time. We opened a single dock door on a fixed schedule, then added warm pallets in known amounts, then forced the compressor staging. After each change we recorded the response of every zone.

Interviewer (Jordan Ellis): What did you learn from those runs?

Subject (Priya Shah, Controls Lead): Two things surprised us. The coupling between zones sharing a rack was much stronger than we assumed, about sixty percent of the disturbance in zone four came from zone three. And the defrost cycle masked everything for about twenty minutes, so any model we fit across a defrost was wrong. We had to split the data into defrost and non-defrost windows before anything worked.

Interviewer (Jordan Ellis): Did the first model you built hold up?

Subject (Priya Shah, Controls Lead): No. Our first attempt was a linear model with fixed coupling terms. It predicted steady conditions well but it failed during receiving, when the product mass changed quickly. The error went back up to about one and a half degrees. So we moved to a model where the coupling terms change with the compressor stage. That second version kept the error under half a degree in eleven of the twelve zones. Zone nine still drifted because it sits next to the loading bay and gets outside air that we were not measuring.

Interviewer (Jordan Ellis): What did you do about zone nine?

Subject (Priya Shah, Controls Lead): We added an outside air temperature sensor near the bay and fed it into the model as a disturbance input. That brought zone nine inside the band as well, but only when the sensor was shaded. In direct sun the reading was useless. We are still working on that part.

Interviewer (Jordan Ellis): Who did the work, and roughly how much time went into it?

Subject (Priya Shah, Controls Lead): Myself, two controls engineers, Marco and Lena, and a data analyst for the model fitting. I would say about sixty percent of the controls team time from April through November went into this. We also spent money on the extra sensors and on the test site operator's time for the scheduled door openings.

Interviewer (Jordan Ellis): At the end of the year, what do you know now that you did not know before?

Subject (Priya Shah, Controls Lead): We now know that the coupling between zones on a shared rack can be identified from deliberate single-variable disturbances, and that the coupling terms have to vary with compressor stage to stay accurate during receiving. We also know that defrost windows have to be modelled separately. None of that was in the literature we started from. What we still do not know is how to handle a disturbance input when the sensor itself is unreliable, which is why the outside air problem carries into next year.

Interviewer (Jordan Ellis): That is very helpful, Priya. Anything else we should capture?

Subject (Priya Shah, Controls Lead): Only that we threw away two approaches along the way. We tried a purely data-driven neural model early on and it could not explain why it made a decision, which the pharmaceutical customers need for their audits. We also tried separate controllers per zone with feed-forward from the neighbours, and it oscillated whenever two neighbours reacted to each other. Both failures shaped the version that finally worked.

toolInput.storyline:
CLIENT_1_BRAND builds controllers for residential solar microgrids, clusters of homes with rooftop solar and batteries tied together. This year's project targeted a predictive load-balancing controller meant to keep voltage stable across the cluster while shifting load and battery charge and discharge, so no single feeder overloads during simultaneous export or demand peaks. Standard grid control approaches assume a central operator and predictable one-way power flow, which did not fit this setting: power flows both directions, generation is intermittent, and there is no real-time trustworthy central meter. The central technological uncertainty was whether cluster-level net load could be forecast accurately enough to act ahead of a voltage event, given how fast cloud cover changes generation output; the team did not know if a useful forecast was achievable at the required timescale.

The team investigated this uncertainty through successive iterations. A rule-based controller using voltage thresholds to trigger battery dispatch was tried first; it oscillated, with batteries fighting each other across homes and producing voltage flicker. This result indicated coordination needed to be predictive rather than reactive. A forecasting model built from historical generation and weather data was then used to drive dispatch; it performed better in steady conditions but degraded during fast partial-cloud transitions because the forecast lagged reality. A third, distributed approach let each home's controller negotiate with neighbours instead of relying on a central forecast; this held voltage much better but introduced a new problem, negotiation failing to converge when communications latency spiked. The distributed negotiation approach was tested in simulation and on a small bench setup, with voltage staying within band in most scenarios, and in simulation it cut voltage excursions by about two-thirds versus the rule-based baseline. The unresolved technological question, convergence guarantees for the negotiation scheme under degraded communications, remains open and is described as next year's work.
